title: Representable3 — Three-Generator Representability Predicate
content: Defines the predicate `Representable3 a b c n` meaning that n can be expressed as a non-negative ℕ-linear combination of the three generators. The predicate is a direct three-generator port of `Representable` from the parent gallery proof `Proofs/FrobeniusNumber.lean`. All seven closure lemmas in this section, the `frobeniusNumber3` definition (S3a), the 2→3 bridge (S3b), the Sylvester upper bound (S3c), and the finiteness theorem (S4) are built on top of this single predicate.
mathContext: $\text{Representable3}(a, b, c, n) := \exists x, y, z \in \mathbb{N}.\; n = ax + by + cz$

title: S2 Closure Block — Seven One-Line Lemmas
content: Seven canonical closure lemmas establishing the basic algebraic structure of `Representable3`: (i) 0 is always representable via the trivial witness (0, 0, 0); (ii) each of the three generators a, b, c is representable via the corresponding unit witness; (iii) if n is representable, then so are n + a, n + b, and n + c (by incrementing the matching coefficient). All seven proofs are one-line `by ring` or `by linarith` arguments. These closure properties bootstrap the inductive structure of the non-representable set and are the direct three-generator analogues of `representable_zero`, `representable_a`, `representable_b`, `representable_add_a`, `representable_add_b` from `Proofs/FrobeniusNumber.lean` (lines 42–69).
relatedConcepts: additive monoid generated by {a, b, c}

title: frobeniusNumber3 — The Three-Generator Frobenius Number as sSup
content: Defines `frobeniusNumber3 a b c` as the supremum of the set of non-representable naturals. The choice of `sSup` (rather than a minimum-of-counterexamples formulation) gracefully handles two degenerate cases via the ℕ-sSup convention `csSup_empty = 0`: (1) when the set is empty (e.g., a = 1, where every n = a*n is representable), and (2) when the set is unbounded (e.g., a = b = c = 0). In both degenerate cases, `frobeniusNumber3` defaults to 0. The trade-off: attainment of the supremum becomes a separate theorem (`not_representable3_frobeniusNumber3_of_nonempty`) requiring `BddAbove` + `Nonempty` hypotheses. The function is marked `noncomputable` because `sSup` on ℕ uses classical choice.
mathContext: $\text{frobeniusNumber3}(a, b, c) := \sup\{n \in \mathbb{N} \mid \neg\,\text{Representable3}(a, b, c, n)\}$, with the ℕ-$\sup$ convention $\sup(\emptyset) = 0$ and $\sup(\text{unbounded}) = 0$.

title: Every n above the Frobenius number is representable (under BddAbove)
content: Proves the defining characterization of the Frobenius number: every n strictly above `frobeniusNumber3 a b c` is representable, **conditional** on the non-representable set being bounded above. The hypothesis `BddAbove` is essential — without it, the sSup defaults to 0 and the statement becomes vacuous (e.g., if a = b = c = 0, every nonzero n is in the non-representable set, but frobeniusNumber3 = 0, so the conclusion `n > 0 → Representable3 0 0 0 n` is false). The proof is by contradiction: if n were non-representable, then n ∈ the set, so n ≤ sSup of the set by `le_csSup` — but then n ≤ frobeniusNumber3, contradicting n > frobeniusNumber3.
mathContext: If $\{m \mid \neg\,\text{Representable3}(a,b,c,m)\}$ is bounded above and $n > \text{frobeniusNumber3}(a,b,c)$, then $\text{Representable3}(a,b,c,n)$.

title: Abstract Upper Bound from Subset-of-Iio
content: Provides the workhorse abstract upper-bound principle: if every non-representable n is < K, then frobeniusNumber3 ≤ K. This is the **plug-in lemma** through which concrete upper bounds (the Sylvester bound in S3c, the eventual Roberts bound in S5+, family-specific bounds in S6+) feed into the structural framework. The proof handles two cases via `by_cases hne` on emptiness: (i) if the non-representable set is nonempty, apply `csSup_le hne` to convert pointwise n ≤ K into sSup ≤ K; (ii) if empty, `csSup_empty = 0 ≤ K` via `bot_le`. This dual handling is what makes the sSup-based definition robust.

title: The sSup is Attained — frobeniusNumber3 is Itself Non-Representable
content: When the non-representable set is bounded above and nonempty, its supremum is a member of the set — i.e., `frobeniusNumber3 a b c` is itself non-representable. This is the precise sense in which the Frobenius number is the *largest* non-representable integer. The proof is a one-line application of `Nat.sSup_mem`, which encodes the well-foundedness of ℕ: a bounded-above nonempty subset of ℕ contains its supremum (this is **false** for ℝ — e.g., the open interval (0, 1) has sSup = 1 not in the set). The auxiliary `representable3_of_two_gen` (collapsing a 3-generator witness with z = 0 to a 2-generator witness) is the bridge lemma used in the next stage (S3b).
mathContext: If $\{m \mid \neg\,\text{Representable3}(a,b,c,m)\}$ is nonempty and bounded above, then $\neg\,\text{Representable3}(a, b, c, \text{frobeniusNumber3}(a, b, c))$.

title: S3b Bridge — Lifting the 2-Generator Sylvester Bound to 3 Generators
content: The conceptual hinge of the entire S3 stack: by zeroing the third coefficient z = 0, the Sylvester 2-generator bound transfers verbatim to 3 generators *without using c at all*. Specifically: for coprime a, b ≥ 1, every n ≥ (a-1)(b-1) is `Representable3 a b c n`, witnessed by (x, y, 0) where (x, y) is the 2-generator witness from the parent `FrobeniusNumber.large_representable`. The proof is a one-liner: destructure the 2-generator witness, then `exact representable3_of_two_gen hxy`. This shows that any non-representable n in the 3-generator setting is **already non-representable as ax + by alone**, so c can only **shrink**, not enlarge, the non-representable set — the precise sense in which adding generators monotonically improves coverage. The import dependency on `Proofs.FrobeniusNumber` was build-blocked under a Mathlib v4.26.0 regression until mechanic PR #19194 cleared it.
mathContext: For $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ with $a, b \ge 1$ and $(a-1)(b-1) \le n$, $\text{Representable3}(a, b, c, n)$ holds, witnessed by the Sylvester 2-generator decomposition $n = ax + by$ with $z = 0$.

title: S3c Concrete Sylvester Upper Bound — The Loose Form
content: Proves `frobeniusNumber3_le_sylvester_bound`: for coprime a, b ≥ 1, `frobeniusNumber3 a b c ≤ (a - 1) * (b - 1)`. The proof combines S3a's `frobeniusNumber3_le_of_subset_Iio` with the **contrapositive** of S3b's bridge: any n not in `Representable3` must satisfy n < (a-1)(b-1) (since otherwise the bridge would force representability). The bound is **loose** — the strictly tighter `≤ (a-1)(b-1) - 1` (matching Sylvester's tight 2-generator $g(a,b) = ab - a - b = (a-1)(b-1) - 1$) requires a case-split on `a = 1 ∨ b = 1` to handle ℕ-subtraction underflow when the non-representable set is empty, deferred to a successor iteration. The loose form is the **unconditional all-cases bound** with a uniform one-line proof via `by_contra` + `push_neg`.
mathContext: For $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ with $a, b \ge 1$, $\text{frobeniusNumber3}(a, b, c) \le (a-1)(b-1)$. The tight Sylvester form would give $\le (a-1)(b-1) - 1 = ab - a - b$, matching the 2-generator value.

title: S4 Finiteness — The Non-Representable Set is Finite
content: Proves `set_non_representable3_finite_of_coprime_ab`: for coprime a, b ≥ 1, the non-representable set $\{n \mid \neg\,\text{Representable3}\,a\,b\,c\,n\}$ is finite. The proof structure mirrors S3c — the same contrapositive of S3b — but feeds it into `Set.Finite.subset Set.finite_Iio ((a-1)*(b-1))` instead of `frobeniusNumber3_le_of_subset_Iio`. Together with the S3a structural API: (i) `Set.Finite.bddAbove` supplies the `BddAbove` hypothesis needed by `representable3_of_gt_frobeniusNumber3_of_bddAbove`; (ii) `not_representable3_frobeniusNumber3_of_nonempty` then establishes sSup-attainment whenever the set is nonempty. This completes the foundational characterization: `frobeniusNumber3` is a genuine maximum (not just a supremum) whenever the non-representable set is nonempty under coprimality of any two generators. The hypothesis is `Nat.Coprime a b` (not the symmetric $\gcd(a, b, c) = 1$) because c plays no role in the Sylvester bound — the asymmetry reflects the strict 2-generator origin of the proof.
mathContext: For $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ with $a, b \ge 1$, $\{n \in \mathbb{N} \mid \neg\,\text{Representable3}(a, b, c, n)\}$ is a finite subset of $[0, (a-1)(b-1))$, hence finite by `Set.finite_Iio` (via `LocallyFiniteOrderBot ℕ`).
